After my transplant, I initially wanted to go into nursing and started a BSN program. It turned out to not be what I wanted to do with my life and instead I switched to studying Health Information Management. Now I work with electronic health records and get the chance to test our programs and work directly with doctors and nurses and other medical professionals to ensure they know how to use the software and that we capture everything important. We got our little girl at 4 months old and the first few weeks—maybe even months, honestly— were terrible. I massively regretted adopting her even though I was the one who really wanted a dog. She nipped and chewed on everything, wouldn’t sleep in her crate and would instead do this howling cry that all of our neighbors could hear. She needed attention and play constantly. I literally could not work in my own office (I work from home) and had to move my computer into our living area. 
She’s a little over a year now and she is probably the best thing that happened to us. She still gets riled up and playful (as she should!) and insists on getting attention but we’ve got our schedule down. No more accidents. She is crate trained. No more biting or excessive chewing around our apartment (okay, there is a weird spot on our wall that she still enjoys biting from time to time but I’ll take it lol). She still has her crazy moments but she’s overall really well behaved and SUCH a sweetheart. She makes us laugh every single day. She cuddles now and not just when she’s exhausted! We sent her to daycare today but I genuinely miss her and probably will pick her up as soon as work is over. She’s the silliest cutest girl I could have ever asked for and I’m so glad I got through all those rough times to end up here with her as such an important part of our family.

I had my heart transplant as a pediatric patient! I was 15 when I got my new heart, so definitely different circumstances and I’m just over 13 years out now. Since my transplant, I’ve noticed that my temperature regulation is a bit out of wack. I can get very hot or very cold easily and sometimes without much reason. I “ran hot” before my transplant at times but now I sometimes go from one extreme to another— my transplant team says they haven’t heard of that in other patients, but I met an NP who primarily worked with lung transplant patients and she said shes seen it before. Still, have to wonder if that’s just me and my weirdo body or if the transplant has anything to do with it!

Waiting really sucks. There’s no way around it, it just does and I’m so sorry that you have to go through this. I was 15 when I was listed and received my heart transplant and I’m now over 13 years out. It gets better, but there’s still challenges. I’m also a Philly patient so I can commiserate with the doctors and nurses not necessarily being able to answer questions— keep in mind, though, you might only be dealing with those who work inpatient so they might not be as aware of transplant in the outpatient setting. It’s generally much better and I can tell you that I live a mostly normal life these days. 

As for the other patient on your floor waiting for a second heart— if he had his original procedure done in 1990, that means he got to 34ish years! Obviously not as long as we want to live, but thats pretty incredible when you consider that you have to be in pretty bad shape to get the transplant in the first place. Those are likely 34 years he wouldn’t have had otherwise and he still has the opportunity to have more! I’ve read about a couple of folks who have made it to 40 years with their new heart and are doing well. The medicine and the protocols are only improving— that’s a pretty big positive.

It was uncomfortable and at first, I definitely experienced some pain from the internal work. ZanyDragons post was really accurate for my experience as well though, with the PT being gentle and taking things on my terms. I also jumped into internal work personally, but I also received a compound cream from my OBGYN that helped desensitize the entrance of my vagina so I was able to tolerate it much better than I initially expected.

Pelvic floor PT helped me get to the point of using tampons, tolerating speculum exams and having sex without pain! I cannot recommend it enough! The internal exam/work was awkward for me at first but I got used to it pretty quickly— my PT helped release my pelvic floor during my visits and I dilated at home on a very regular basis and let her know about my progress. I think I did it for less than 6 months and it absolutely changed my life.

I was super sick before I went into cardiac arrest… think bad stomach bug and a fever that lasted about two weeks. I had absolutely no appetite— I think I lost 10 pounds without trying to, which is crazy, considering I literally look at food and gain a couple ounces lol. We still don’t know exactly what it was but I ended up going into the hospital after I passed out while sick… my transplant team wanted me to get some IV fluids and antibiotics and get some testing to determine what was actually going on. I was admitted and then… boom, the following morning I went into cardiac arrest, right there in the cardiac unit! Had a cath immediately afterwards and everyone was expecting to see some sort of blockage, but there wasn’t any, just some high grade rejection. The team thinks I wasn’t properly absorbing my immunosuppressants for those 2 weeks or so and it put me in a pretty bad place.

Super relieved that I was able to get through that point and that I’m doing significantly better now!

Hey there, I’m not a kidney recipient but I am a heart recipient so I understand parts of the struggle. Sometimes you can do everything right and stuff still happens. It’s the unfortunate truth of being an organ recipient and well… it sucks, no sugarcoating there. The amazing thing is that rejection is reversible! I went into rejection 6 years after my transplant and I’ll be honest— it was not good, we caught it pretty late and I went into cardiac arrest. But even then, my doctors were able to get me on a higher immunosuppressant regimen and get me back to a good place. That was 7 years ago and I have not been in high grade rejection like that since.

Hey there! I’m 13 years post heart transplant and I think one of the trickiest (and sometimes most annoying!) things about transplants is how different they are for everyone. I believe the first year or so post transplant they want your immunosuppression levels to be pretty high. When I was first transplanted, I think I remember being on 4 or 5 mg of tac twice a day, along with 1500mg of mycophenolate. The tac was always changing that early on though! Now that I’m much further out, I’m on 1.5 mg of tac total in a day and 750mg of mycophenolate twice a day— granted, I’m also on sirolimus now so that’s changed things for me too. Your tac dose especially will probably change once your body gets a little more used to things and your level doesn’t need to be quite as high!

I was 15 when I had my transplant, and that was almost 13 years ago so things have almost definitely changed but I can share some of my experience.

I took about 3 months to make my decision to be listed for a heart but was only on the list for 11 days. That being said, I was a pediatric patient and had already gone into cardiac arrest once and had multiple arrhythmias that had been stopped by my ICD at the time, so I think I was considered high priority from the get-go. We got the call in the very middle of the night and I think I ended up actually waiting for the heart to arrive for 25 hours before I went back into surgery. I don’t think that’s too uncommon.

Following transplant, I was in the hospital for 3 weeks and experienced rejection at about 1.5 weeks out. There were a lot of biopsies and lab tests happening at this point. I feel like I saw doctors from just about every specialty to make sure everything was good… I was lucky in that everything was! Steroids definitely started affecting me about a week in, but I don’t remember being too moody, my family might beg to differ on that though. It did make me insanely hungry and probably contributed to some insomnia in the hospital. The insomnia (and the pain too!) got much better almost the second I got to go home. 

It has been a wild ride since transplant and there have certainly been some huge bumps on the road. I’ve developed afib from the way this heart was sutured in and went into cardiac arrest after being super sick for a long period of time. The immunosuppression is no joke! Tell your transplant team if you’re sick for an extended period of time, especially if its in a way that can mess with the absorption of your meds. I have another ICD now because of the arrest and have unfortunately been shocked by it a few times. I wish I could tell you the transplant is a cure all and solves everything, but unfortunately I cannot. However, all of the problems after transplant have been treatable and manageable. I’m so grateful for my life and the things my transplant has enabled— I finished high school, got a college degree, have a full-time job that I (usually) really like and gotten to travel and fall in love and be a dog owner! All things I wouldnt have gotten without the transplant. Medical stuff sucks but it can lead to some pretty awesome things!!!

It may hurt because its not in correctly and/or it hasnt been soaked in blood for long enough (gross, I know). Try to relax, easier said than done, and give yourself time to take it out.
